records.name: Baring family
records.scaleNote: Not slave traders themselves, but per UCL LBS the family's partners were mortgagees and compensation counter-claimants on Caribbean and Guiana estates, and Alexander Baring was reported to have received compensation for almost 500 enslaved people across four estates.
records.origins: Descended from Johann Baring, a Bremen wool merchant who settled in Exeter in 1717. His sons John and Francis founded a London merchant house in 1762 that grew into Barings Bank.
records.role_summary: Sir Francis Baring (1740–1810) built the family fortune partly through West India finance, and his son Alexander Baring (1774–1848) repeatedly opposed abolition in Parliament. Through the family firm the Barings lent to slave-owners and pursued compensation money owed to them at emancipation.

roleDetail.t: Sir Francis Baring and West India credit.
roleDetail.d: Per UCL LBS, Sir Francis had financial interests in Caribbean sugar and slavery, including the Bogue estate in Jamaica, probably as mortgagee.
MP from 1806 and later Lord Ashburton, he spoke repeatedly against emancipation; the Devon and Exeter Institution notes compensation for almost 500 enslaved people across four estates.
Partners Thomas, John and Francis Baring pursued compensation for the enslaved people of the Berbice slave-owner Wolfert Katz, a heavy debtor of the firm.

records.legacy: The family produced several peerages (Ashburton, Northbrook, Revelstoke, Cromer) and senior figures in British public life, including a Governor of the Bank of England (the 3rd Earl of Cromer). The family bank collapsed in 1995. Christ's College, Cambridge and the National Gallery now describe Baring links to slavery in their own legacy research.

legacyDetail.d: Christ's College's Legacies of Enslavement pages and the National Gallery's biography of Alexander Baring record the family's ties to slave-ownership.
The Baring Archive backs a University of Leeds PhD, funded by Baring Asset Management and ING, mapping the firm's involvement with the slave economy.

records.today: The peerages of Baron Ashburton, Baron Northbrook, Baron Revelstoke and Earl of Cromer are still held by Baring descendants, though the family no longer controls a bank. Barings collapsed in 1995 and was bought by ING for £1. The family name lives on in the Baring Foundation (a charity set up in 1969), the Baring Archive, and the asset manager Barings. Baring Asset Management and ING fund a University of Leeds PhD, begun in 2022, on Baring Brothers' involvement with slavery. Current Baring peers include the 6th Baron Northbrook, the 8th Baron Ashburton, the 4th Earl of Cromer, the 7th Baron Revelstoke and the 2nd Baron Howick of Glendale; the last hereditary Baring seat in the Lords (Lord Northbrook's) ended on 29 April 2026 under the House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Act 2026.

records.name: Baring Brothers & Co. (Barings Bank)
records.scaleNote: One of 'the City's two dominant merchant banks' (per UCL LBS); it placed c. $2.5m in Louisiana planter-bank bonds backed by mortgages on enslaved people in 1828 and financed 60% of the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.
records.origins: Founded in London in 1762 as John and Francis Baring & Co.; renamed Baring Brothers & Co. in 1807. It became a leading financier of Atlantic trade and of the young United States.
records.role_summary: Barings did not ship captives, but its credit ran through the slave economy: it lent to Caribbean and Guiana slave-owners, collected their compensation in the 1830s, and sold bonds of Louisiana banks whose capital rested on mortgaged enslaved people. It also handled much of the Atlantic cotton trade.

roleDetail.d: With Hope & Co. of Amsterdam, Barings bought the US bonds used to pay France, taking 60% of the risk; Alexander Baring carried the bonds across the Atlantic.
Barings sold c. $2.5m of 5% bonds of the Consolidated Association of the Planters of Louisiana, whose shareholders mortgaged land and enslaved people.
Per UCL LBS, the partners successfully intercepted compensation on the Wolfert Katz estates in Berbice, British Guiana, and lent to New Orleans slave-owner Burrill Carnes against slave property.

records.legacy: Barings survived a near-collapse in 1890 with a Bank of England rescue, but failed in 1995 after rogue-trader losses and was bought by Dutch bank ING for £1. The Barings name continues in Barings LLC (asset management) and the Baring Foundation; the firm's records are held by The Baring Archive in London.

legacyDetail.d: ING absorbed the banking business in 1995; the archive and a charitable foundation survive under the Baring name.
The Baring Archive hosts a funded Leeds PhD (from 2023) on the firm's slavery links; no corporate apology had been issued as of this writing.

records.name: Lloyds Banking Group
records.scaleNote: Not to be confused with Lloyd's of London. Its documented link is through predecessor the London & Brazilian Bank (1862), which held enslaved Afro-Brazilians as loan security (per Durham research), plus slavery-derived wealth among Scottish predecessor banks (per Mullen, 2023).
records.origins: Lloyds Bank began as Taylors & Lloyds, a Birmingham Quaker bank, in 1765; it absorbed hundreds of banks, including the Bank of London & South America, and merged with HBOS (Bank of Scotland, Halifax) in 2009.
records.role_summary: Its predecessor, the London & Brazilian Bank, lent in Brazil after British emancipation and, per historian Joe Mulhern, knowingly accepted enslaved people as collateral and sometimes forced their sale to settle debts. Other predecessor banks had partners and directors who received 1830s slave-owner compensation.

roleDetail.d: Mulhern's Durham research shows the London & Brazilian Bank held mortgages secured on enslaved people in Brazil, where slavery lasted until 1888.
A 2023 University of Glasgow study by Stephen Mullen concluded that the group's commercial success was 'predicated upon' Atlantic slavery in the 18th–19th centuries.

records.legacy: Lloyds Banking Group is today one of the UK's largest retail banks (Lloyds, Halifax, Bank of Scotland). In June 2020, after the Telegraph reported predecessor-bank links in the UCL LBS database, a spokeswoman said that while 'we have much within our heritage to be proud of, we can't be proud of it all', adding 'We stand against racism, slavery and discrimination in all its forms'; it issued no formal apology or reparations scheme.

legacyDetail.d: Lloyds acknowledged it 'can't be proud of it all' and pledged to do 'more' and 'better' on diversity (as reported by the Telegraph and Leasing Life, July 2020); reparation pledges that month came from Lloyd's of London and Greene King, not Lloyds Bank.

lineage.name: Sampson Lloyd II and John Taylor
lineage.note: A Quaker iron founder and a Unitarian Birmingham manufacturer who each put about £2,000 into the private bank Taylors & Lloyds at Dale End in June 1765. No direct slavery link to the two founders has been documented; the group's links run through later predecessor banks.

lineage.name: Lloyds & Co. / Lloyds Banking Company
lineage.note: The Taylor family left in 1852 and the firm became Lloyds & Co., a joint-stock company in 1865 and Lloyds Bank Limited by 1889, which went on to absorb hundreds of English banks.

lineage.name: London & Brazilian Bank
lineage.note: British bank in Brazil that, per Joe Mulhern (LSE), knowingly took enslaved people as loan collateral until 1888; its president John White Cater had received British compensation on five Jamaican claims. Lloyds bought it in 1923 and it became part of the Bank of London & South America.

lineage.name: Bank of London & South America (BOLSA) / Lloyds Bank International
lineage.note: Merger of the London & Brazilian and London & River Plate banks; fully absorbed into Lloyds as Lloyds Bank International, carrying the Brazilian business into the group.

lineage.name: Other UK predecessor banks (eight named in LBS)
lineage.note: UCL's Legacies of British Slavery database links eight former Lloyds-group companies to people who claimed or received compensation under the 1833 Act.

lineage.name: Lloyds TSB and HBOS (Bank of Scotland, Halifax)
lineage.note: Lloyds merged with TSB in 1995 and took over HBOS in 2009, bringing in the Bank of Scotland (1695) and the Trustee Savings Banks, whose Scottish commercial success Stephen Mullen (2023) found was tied to Atlantic slavery.

lineage.name: Lloyds Banking Group plc
lineage.note: The current listed group (Lloyds, Halifax, Bank of Scotland, Scottish Widows).

records.today: Lloyds Banking Group plc is one of the UK's largest retail banking groups (Lloyds Bank, Halifax, Bank of Scotland, Scottish Widows). In June 2020, after press reports drawing on the UCL LBS database, a spokeswoman said 'we can't be proud of it all' and that the bank stands 'against racism, slavery and discrimination in all its forms'. A 2023 University of Glasgow study by Stephen Mullen for the Corra Foundation (a charity funded from Lloyds TSB) concluded that the group's commercial success depended in part on Atlantic slavery; no formal corporate apology or reparations scheme has been documented.

records.name: NatWest Group (formerly Royal Bank of Scotland Group)
records.scaleNote: Descends from more than 100 banks founded in the 18th–early 19th centuries; its own heritage research shows predecessor partners took plantation mortgages, owned a Grenada plantation (Hankey & Co, 1767–72) and received 1830s compensation.
records.origins: NatWest began trading in 1970 from older banks including Hankey & Co (1685), Smith, Payne & Smiths (1758) and Prescott's Bank (1766); RBS took it over in 2000 and the group renamed itself NatWest Group in 2020.
records.role_summary: Predecessor banks lent to West India planters on the security of land and enslaved people; Smith, Payne & Smiths once helped fund the purchase of enslaved people for a plantation, and its partners received substantial compensation. A director of the London and Westminster Bank, John Stewart, was also a compensation recipient.

roleDetail.d: In 1766 it took a mortgage on a Grenada plantation and owned it, with its enslaved people, until 1772; four partners later received compensation.
Accepted plantation mortgages in the 1810s–20s and in one case financed the purchase of enslaved people, per NatWest's heritage hub.
RBS's 2006 report (updated 2009), prepared for US disclosure laws via its Citizens Bank subsidiary, found predecessor directors had owned enslaved people.

records.legacy: NatWest Group is a FTSE 100 bank (NatWest, Royal Bank of Scotland, Coutts). In June 2020 an RBS spokeswoman told the Telegraph these 'important and painful issues have a place in our history', said the bank had researched its slavery links 'very extensively and thoroughly' for 15 years, and that a BAME-led taskforce would consider what more it could do, including contributions to BAME groups. Its Heritage Hub publishes an 'Enslavement and Colonialism' page, but no formal apology or reparations commitment has been made.

legacyDetail.d: RBS said it was examining further action, including possible contributions to BAME groups (Fortune and Leasing Life reporting the Telegraph); no reparations programme followed.
The heritage page states there is 'no doubt' that people enriched by slavery were among predecessor banks' customers.
Three partners of its Bristol predecessor banks were founder members of Bristol's 1788 abolition committee.

records.name: HSBC (Midland Bank predecessors)
records.scaleNote: HSBC's own 2020–23 review of c. 1,700 leaders of 100+ UK predecessor banks found direct slavery links at five: Leyland & Bullins, Moss & Co, City Bank, Galton & James (unconfirmed predecessor) and London Joint Stock Bank.
records.origins: HSBC was founded in Hong Kong in 1865 and bought Britain's Midland Bank in 1992. Midland had absorbed many older English banks, including two founded in Liverpool in 1807 by men enriched by the slave trade.
records.role_summary: The slavery links are through founders and leaders of predecessor banks: Thomas Leyland helped finance at least 69 slaving voyages (per HSBC), John Moss shipped and held enslaved people in the Bahamas and Demerara, and London Joint Stock Bank's first manager, George Pollard, was a trustee-awardee of £2,416 compensation for Colhoun's estate, Nevis (per UCL LBS).

roleDetail.d: Leyland & Bullins and Moss & Co were both founded in 1807, the year Britain banned the slave trade, by men whose wealth came partly from it.
HSBC counted investing in voyages, owning enslaved people or receiving compensation; other investigations were said to be ongoing.

records.legacy: HSBC is one of the world's largest banks. On its history site it states that it 'regrets the past actions and activities of individuals associated with these predecessor banks and the harm they caused', but it has made no reparations commitment.

legacyDetail.d: The research concluded in the first half of 2023 and is published on history.hsbc.com under 'Lessons from history'.

records.name: Moss family of Liverpool (John Moss)
records.scaleNote: Per UCL LBS, the Moss brothers inherited c. 1,000 enslaved people in the Bahamas in 1820, moved 603 of them to Demerara in 1821–25, and John Moss was awarded £40,353 for Anna Regina estate.
records.origins: A Liverpool merchant family partly enriched by the transatlantic slave trade. John Moss joined his father's firm and in 1807 founded the bank Moss, Dales & Rogers.
records.role_summary: John and his brothers inherited enslaved people from their uncle James Moss and, under licence, forcibly moved hundreds of them from the Bahamas to cotton and sugar estates in Demerara, where an intra-Caribbean transfer still separated families. John Moss was paid one of the larger compensation awards.

roleDetail.d: Of 1,762 people imported under licence into Demerara–Essequibo in 1821–25, 603 were sent from the Bahamas by John, Henry and James Moss (per LBS).
John Moss was awardee of £40,353 18s 3d for Anna Regina, British Guiana.
A biography says Moss worked with Sir John Gladstone on the planters' compensation campaign.

records.legacy: John Moss became first chairman of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, an early icon of industrial Britain. His bank became the North Western Bank, then part of Midland Bank, now HSBC UK, which in 2023 publicly listed his slavery links.

legacyDetail.d: Moss & Co (1826) → North Western Bank (1864) → London and Midland Bank (1897) → HSBC (1992).

records.name: Drax family (Drax Hall, Barbados)
records.scaleNote: James Drax pioneered large-scale sugar in Barbados in the 1640s with c. 200 enslaved Africans by the early 1650s; at abolition the family claimed £4,293 for 189 people on Drax Hall (per UCL LBS); the family still owns the estate.
records.base: Drax Hall, St George, Barbados / Charborough, Dorset
records.origins: James Drax was an English settler who arrived in Barbados in the 1620s. He was among the first planters to make sugar work on a large scale there, and he bought African captives to do it.
records.role_summary: The Draxes created one of the earliest and longest-lived English slave plantations, holding enslaved people at Drax Hall from the 1640s until 1834, plus a large Jamaica estate. Historian Hilary Beckles has called Drax Hall a 'killing field' where tens of thousands died, though death-toll figures are estimates.

roleDetail.d: Drax Hall (c. 1650) is one of the oldest surviving houses in the Americas and the site where the gang-labour sugar system took shape in Barbados.
J.S.W.S. Erle-Drax claimed £4,293 12s 6d for 189 enslaved people at Drax Hall (LBS claim Barbados 3784).
Beckles's estimate of up to 30,000 deaths is widely quoted; other accounts give 'thousands'.

records.legacy: Richard Drax, Conservative MP for South Dorset 2010–2024, inherited the c. 617-acre Drax Hall estate on his father's death in 2017 (probate of the Barbados holding was still being completed in 2021) and the family seat at Charborough. Barbados's government considered seeking reparations from him in 2022; a 2024 plan to buy 50 acres for housing (reportedly c. £3m) was paused after public outcry. He has called his ancestors' role 'deeply regrettable' but says no one today can be held responsible.

legacyDetail.t: First individual reparations claim by a state.
legacyDetail.d: A 2022 Barbados cabinet paper reportedly proposed asking Drax to contribute land for a museum and housing, with legal action as an option.
No settlement had been announced as of 2025 reporting.

records.name: General Sir James Duff
records.scaleNote: Owner of the Grange sugar estate, Hanover, Jamaica (1832–39), for which £4,101 0s 1d was awarded (claim Jamaica Hanover 455, per UCL LBS); LBS registers 211–221 enslaved people there in 1830–32.
records.origins: A Scottish army officer and MP for Banffshire, of the family of the Earls Fife. Like many Scottish gentry he held Jamaican plantation property.
records.role_summary: Duff owned the Grange sugar estate in Jamaica and was compensated as its owner when slavery ended. He is a direct example of how 1830s compensation money flowed into the British landed and political class.

records.name: Charles McGarel and the Hogg family (Viscounts Hailsham)
records.scaleNote: Charles McGarel was among the largest compensation beneficiaries: e.g. £9,751 for 184 people on Nouvelle Flandres, Demerara; partners in Hall, McGarel received almost £100,000 for nearly 1,000 people (per UCL LBS / Wikipedia).
records.origins: Charles McGarel, from Larne in Ulster, became a Demerara merchant and slave-owner. He married into the Hogg family; his brother-in-law Quintin Hogg entered the West India sugar trade through him.
records.role_summary: McGarel owned and mortgaged estates in Demerara and Berbice, petitioned in 1826 against compulsory manumission, and collected large compensation sums. Quintin Hogg later ran Demerara sugar estates worked by indentured labourers after emancipation.

roleDetail.d: McGarel was one of 65 absentee owners and mortgagees petitioning the Privy Council in 1826 against compulsory manumission in Demerara and Berbice.
McGarel left his estate to brother-in-law James Hogg on condition he added 'McGarel' to his name; the name passed into the Hailsham line.

records.legacy: McGarel's money built Larne Town Hall, which Amnesty International asked to be renamed in 2020. Quintin Hogg founded the Regent Street Polytechnic (now University of Westminster); his son and grandson were the 1st and 2nd Viscounts Hailsham, both Lord Chancellors. How far McGarel wealth funded the Polytechnic is debated.

legacyDetail.d: Amnesty called for McGarel Town Hall to be renamed over his slavery links.
Connections between slavery-derived money and later philanthropy are drawn by LBS but not quantified.

records.name: Moses Taylor
records.scaleNote: By the Civil War his firm's network covered at least 24 Cuban estates that profited from the labour of thousands of enslaved people (per Princeton & Slavery Project).
records.origins: A New York clerk with the Howland shipping firm, he set up as a sugar broker in 1832, aged 26, handling Cuban growers' sugar.
records.role_summary: Taylor sold Cuban sugar in New York, extended credit and investment advice to Cuban planters, and banked their money in the US, while Cuba still imported African captives illegally. His partners and clients included Drake Brothers of Havana and Tomás Terry, men tied to the slave trade.

roleDetail.d: Historian Roland Ely showed that Taylor acted as banker and agent for slave-owning Cuban sugar planters (1833–1868).
He led City Bank of New York from 1856 to 1882; his businesses held accounts there, which Citi says let the bank profit indirectly from enslaved labour.

records.legacy: City Bank became National City Bank and then Citigroup. Taylor's grandson Moses Taylor Pyne was one of Princeton University's leading benefactors, a link documented by the Princeton & Slavery Project. His papers are held by the New York Public Library.

legacyDetail.d: Pyne's gifts to Princeton derived in part from the Taylor sugar fortune.

records.today: CSX Corporation, based in Jacksonville, Florida, is one of the largest US freight railroads and still runs over track built or worked by enslaved people, such as the RF&P Subdivision. The 2002 reparations claims against it were dismissed in 2004–05, and no CSX apology or historical study of its predecessors' use of enslaved labour has been found.

records.name: Norfolk Southern (predecessor railroads)
records.scaleNote: Successor to Southern Railway and Norfolk & Western lines, some of whose antebellum predecessors leased and purchased enslaved workers; lawsuits in 2002 alleged this but no total is documented.
records.origins: Formed in 1982 from the Southern Railway and the Norfolk & Western, which had absorbed dozens of pre-Civil War Southern lines.
records.role_summary: Antebellum predecessor lines in the South rented enslaved men for construction and maintenance, and some owned enslaved workers. Norfolk Southern was named in 2002 suits as their successor.

roleDetail.d: A class action led by former NAACP official Richard Barber Sr. named Norfolk Southern, New York Life and Brown Brothers Harriman.
Precise numbers for NS predecessor lines are not established in sources found here.

records.legacy: Norfolk Southern is a major US freight railroad. The reparations suits against it were dismissed with the consolidated 2004–05 rulings; the company has issued no apology.

legacyDetail.d: Railroad slavery is now studied by historians, but no company-commissioned report like the banks' exists.

lineage.name: South Carolina Canal & Rail Road Company
lineage.note: Its 136-mile Charleston–Hamburg line (1833) was built largely by enslaved labourers, and enslaved firemen worked its engines, including the Best Friend of Charleston, which exploded in 1831.

lineage.name: South Carolina Railroad
lineage.note: Renamed company that hired enslaved people from nearby plantations and bought 89 African Americans between 1845 and 1860 to maintain the line.

lineage.name: South Carolina & Georgia Railroad
lineage.note: Reorganised successor, absorbed into the Southern Railway system.

lineage.name: Southern Railway
lineage.note: Southern system that gathered dozens of antebellum lines, including the old South Carolina Railroad.

lineage.name: Norfolk & Western Railway
lineage.note: Virginia-based system whose antebellum predecessor lines also operated in the slave South; its own use of enslaved labour is less well documented.

lineage.name: Norfolk Southern Corporation
lineage.note: Formed by merging Southern and N&W; sued in 2002 as successor to slave-labour railroads.

records.today: Norfolk Southern Corporation, based in Atlanta, is a major US freight railroad. Its oldest strand, the South Carolina Canal & Rail Road, is celebrated in railroad history for the Best Friend of Charleston, though state histories record that enslaved people built, fired and maintained it. The 2002 reparations suits were dismissed, and no company apology or historical study has been found.

records.name: Brooks Brothers
records.scaleNote: Made livery for enslaved coachmen and footmen in Southern households; a surviving coat worn by a young man enslaved by Dr William Newton Mercer is held by The Historic New Orleans Collection. The volume of this trade is unknown because company records are private.
records.origins: Founded in New York in 1818 by Henry Sands Brooks; it became America's oldest clothing brand.
records.role_summary: Brooks Brothers sold livery made for enslaved domestic workers, including coats with family-crest buttons, to wealthy Southern planters. Historian Jonathan Michael Square calls livery an extensive part of its 19th-century business.

roleDetail.d: Two Brooks Brothers livery coats from the Mercer household (Mississippi/New Orleans), sold through the firm's livery department c. 1857–65 and acquired by The Historic New Orleans Collection in 2013, survive as rare material evidence.

records.legacy: Brooks Brothers still trades (bought out of bankruptcy in 2020 by SPARC Group). Researchers note it has not publicly acknowledged this history, and its archive remains closed to them.

legacyDetail.d: Square's research into the scale of the trade has been limited by lack of access to company records.

sources.label: Vestoj — A Stain on an All-American Brand (Jonathan Michael Square)
The Historic New Orleans Collection — Enslaved servant's coat loan to the Met
Wikipedia — Brooks Brothers

lineage.name: Henry Sands Brooks
lineage.note: Opened H. & D. H. Brooks & Co. at Catherine and Cherry Streets, New York, on 7 April 1818; the firm passed to his four sons on his death in 1833.

lineage.name: The four Brooks sons
lineage.note: They renamed the firm Brooks Brothers in 1850, built its ready-to-wear and livery trade, and in 1853 it appeared among creditors in 'The Tailor's Appeal' over unpaid bills from Southern customers.

lineage.name: Dr William Newton Mercer household, New Orleans
lineage.note: Two Brooks Brothers livery coats with Mercer falcon-crest buttons, now at The Historic New Orleans Collection, were probably made for young enslaved domestic servants.

lineage.name: Winthrop Holley Brooks
lineage.note: Last Brooks family member to run the company; on his retirement it was sold.

lineage.name: Garfinckel's, Allied Stores, Marks & Spencer
lineage.note: Julius Garfinckel & Co. bought it in 1946, Allied Stores took over in 1981 and Marks & Spencer owned it from 1988.

lineage.name: Retail Brand Alliance (Claudio Del Vecchio)
lineage.note: Bought from M&S in 2001; filed for Chapter 11 in July 2020.

lineage.name: SPARC Group / Catalyst Brands
lineage.note: Authentic Brands Group and Simon Property Group's SPARC bought it in 2020; since 2025 it is part of Catalyst Brands (with JCPenney).

records.today: Brooks Brothers trades as a brand of Catalyst Brands. Historian Jonathan Michael Square writes that the company has not publicly acknowledged its sale of livery to slaveholding households and did not respond to his requests to see its archive. No Brooks family descendants have spoken publicly about the link.

records.name: Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations
records.scaleNote: Received and managed Haiti's 1825 indemnity (150m francs, reduced to 90m in 1838) for former colonists for about a century; the NYT (2022) estimated c. 112m francs was actually paid, c. $560m today.
records.origins: A French state financial institution founded in 1816 to hold public and legal deposits.
records.role_summary: Under Charles X's 1825 ordinance Haiti had to pay its indemnity into the Caisse, which distributed it to former Saint-Domingue colonists as compensation for lost property, including enslaved people. Haiti borrowed from French banks such as CIC to keep paying.

roleDetail.d: The Caisse administered the indemnity from 1825 to c. 1925, per a 2025 French civil-society letter citing its archives.
2025 research in the Caisse's archives suggests the French Treasury may itself have gained from the payments.

records.legacy: The Caisse des Dépôts is today France's public financial institution, managing hundreds of billions of euros. On the 200th anniversary in 2025 President Macron announced a joint French–Haitian commission of historians to examine the indemnity; France has not agreed to restitution.

legacyDetail.d: Campaigners, including France's Foundation for the Memory of Slavery, urged France to recognise and repair the indemnity's injustice.

lineage.name: Restoration finance law of 1816
lineage.note: Louis XVIII's government created the Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations to hold public and court-ordered deposits.

lineage.name: Charles X's ordinance of 17 April 1825
lineage.note: Recognised Haiti's independence in exchange for 150 million francs in five instalments, payable to the Caisse for distribution to former colonists.

lineage.name: Ternaux Gandolphe et Cie and the Laffitte consortium
lineage.note: Paris bankers who arranged and bought Haiti's 1825 bond, creating the 'double debt' of indemnity plus loan.

lineage.name: Former Saint-Domingue colonists
lineage.note: Ex-planters and heirs who received payments through the Caisse as compensation for lost property, including enslaved people.

lineage.name: 1838 treaties
lineage.note: France cut the total to 90 million francs, payable over 30 years; France acknowledged it as paid in 1888.

lineage.name: Crédit Industriel et Commercial (CIC)
lineage.note: Lent Haiti money in 1874–75 to finish paying the indemnity and in 1880 set up the Paris-run National Bank of Haiti.

lineage.name: National City Bank of New York
lineage.note: After 1922 Haiti's French-era debt was owed to American investors; per the New York Times (2022) Haiti's last payment went to National City Bank in 1947.

lineage.name: Groupe Caisse des Dépôts
lineage.note: The same public institution, today France's main public financial group.

records.today: The Caisse des Dépôts is today France's public financial group, controlling bodies such as La Poste and Bpifrance. In 2025 Pierre-Yves Bocquet of the Fondation pour la mémoire de l'esclavage used documents in the Caisse's archives to argue that the French Treasury may itself have profited from the 'double debt'. In 2025 France set up a joint Franco-Haitian commission of historians on the indemnity's impact; restitution has not been agreed.

records.name: Royal Exchange Assurance
records.scaleNote: One of only two chartered corporate marine insurers (with London Assurance) from 1720 to 1824, though Lloyd's held c. 75–90% of the market; the slave and West India trades made up c. 41% of British marine insurance in the 1790s (per Pearson & Richardson, Journal of Economic History, 2019).
records.origins: Chartered by Act of Parliament in 1720, the same Bubble Act year as the South Sea scheme, together with London Assurance, to sell marine and fire insurance.
records.role_summary: As a marine insurer during the peak of the British slave trade it sold cover in a market where slave voyages and slave-grown produce were major lines of business. Its fire business also insured Caribbean plantation property, including dwellings of the enslaved.

roleDetail.d: A surviving 1773 Royal Exchange policy for a Barbados property lists slave dwellings among insured buildings.
Historians (Pearson & Richardson) document chartered insurers' role, but the company's own share of slaving cover is not quantified.

records.legacy: Royal Exchange merged with Guardian Assurance in 1968 to form Guardian Royal Exchange, which French insurer AXA bought in 1999. UCL's LBS database links several of its directors and a deputy governor to slavery; unlike Lloyd's of London in 2020, no specific apology for Royal Exchange Assurance has been found.

legacyDetail.d: Now part of AXA's UK business.

lineage.name: 'Onslow's Bubble' promoters (Richard Onslow, 1st Baron Onslow)
lineage.note: Royal Exchange Assurance grew out of an insurance scheme promoted under Lord Onslow, who is usually named as its first governor when it was chartered in 1720.

lineage.name: Royal charter of 1720 (Bubble Act)
lineage.note: With London Assurance, one of two companies granted marine-insurance charters in the same Act that served the South Sea scheme.

lineage.name: Directors and a deputy governor in LBS
lineage.note: UCL's Legacies of British Slavery database links three directors and one deputy governor to slavery.

lineage.name: Guardian Royal Exchange Assurance
lineage.note: Formed when Royal Exchange Assurance combined with the Guardian Assurance Company in 1968.

lineage.name: AXA (Sun Life & Provincial Holdings)
lineage.note: AXA bought Guardian Royal Exchange for c.$5.7bn in February 1999 and folded it into its UK arm Sun Life & Provincial Holdings, selling the life business to Aegon. It was not part of Sun Alliance, which merged with Royal Insurance to form RSA in 1996.

lineage.name: AXA UK
lineage.note: The French group AXA's UK insurance business holds the old general-insurance line.

records.today: Royal Exchange Assurance's business sits today within the French insurer AXA (its UK arm). When Lloyd's, Aviva and RSA acknowledged slave-trade links in 2020, AXA was named for its Guardian Royal Exchange inheritance but was unavailable to comment, and no apology specific to Royal Exchange Assurance has been found. Its archives are held at London Metropolitan Archives (CLC/B/107).

records.name: Elihu Yale
records.scaleNote: As President of Madras for the East India Company (1687–92) he oversaw a port where the Company sanctioned and regulated an Indian Ocean slave trade; how much his own fortune came from it is disputed.
records.origins: Born in Boston and raised in London, he joined the East India Company as a clerk and rose to govern Fort St George, Madras, where he grew rich through private trade.
records.role_summary: This is the Indian Ocean, not the Atlantic, trade: Yale's administration in Madras sanctioned the sale and shipment of enslaved people, and David Blight's 2024 history argues part of his fortune came from trafficking. His 1718 gift of goods funded the college that took his name.

roleDetail.d: Blight's Yale and Slavery (2024) argues the Company's Madras office 'sanctioned and regulated' the Indian Ocean slave trade, that Yale played a 'key leadership role' in it, and that part of his fortune came from buying and selling people.
Some historians argue the evidence does not show Yale was personally a slave trader.

records.legacy: Yale University, named for him in 1718, apologised in February 2024 for its early leaders' ties to slavery. A 1708 portrait of Yale with an enslaved child in a silver collar was removed from a Yale boardroom in 2007.

legacyDetail.d: Yale kept the name while publishing the history.

lineage.name: Theophilus Eaton
lineage.note: Married Elihu's grandmother Anne Yale (née Lloyd), making him stepfather to David Yale; Eaton co-founded the New Haven colony, where Yale College later settled.

lineage.name: David Yale
lineage.note: A Boston merchant and attorney who moved the family to London, where Elihu grew up.

lineage.name: Ursula Knight
lineage.note: Elihu Yale's mother.

lineage.name: Catherine Elford Hynmers
lineage.note: Widow of the Company official Joseph Hynmers and daughter of a Levant merchant; her first husband's estate is thought to have added to Yale's Madras fortune.

lineage.name: Hieronima de Paiva
lineage.note: Widow of the Madras diamond trader Jacques de Paiva, whom Yale took in and with whom he had a son, Charles.

lineage.name: David Yale (son)
lineage.note: Elihu's only legitimate son died as a child, leaving no male heir to the name.

lineage.name: Katherine, Anne and Ursula Yale
lineage.note: Katherine married Dudley North of Glemham Hall, Anne married Lord James Cavendish, and Ursula did not marry; his wealth passed mainly through them.

lineage.name: Yale College (Yale University)
lineage.note: Took his name after his 1718 gift of goods and books, arranged through Cotton Mather and Jeremiah Dummer.

records.today: Yale University carries his name. In February 2024 it apologised for its early leaders' ties to slavery, alongside David Blight's history of Yale and slavery. Yale is buried at St Giles' Church, Wrexham, near his Plas Grono estate. No publicly documented present-day descendants have been identified with the link; his line passed through his daughters into the North and Cavendish families.

records.name: London & Brazilian Bank
records.description: British bank formed in London in 1862 to lend in Brazil, where slavery lasted until 1888. Historian Joe Mulhern showed it knowingly held enslaved Afro-Brazilians as security for loans and sometimes forced their sale; through the Bank of London & South America it is a predecessor of Lloyds Banking Group.

records.name: Farmer-Paellmann reparations lawsuits (2002–2006)
records.description: In March 2002 activist Deadria Farmer-Paellmann sued Aetna, FleetBoston and CSX in federal court in Brooklyn on behalf of descendants of the enslaved; similar suits named Lehman, New York Life, Norfolk Southern and others. The cases were consolidated in Chicago and dismissed in 2004–05 as raising a 'political question', a ruling largely upheld on appeal in 2006.

records.name: Harvard & the Legacy of Slavery report and fund (2022)
records.description: Report published 26 April 2022 finding that Harvard leaders, faculty and staff enslaved more than 70 people from 1636 until Massachusetts abolition, and that donors' fortunes came from slavery and slave-produced goods. President Lawrence Bacow committed $100 million to a Legacy of Slavery Fund for descendant outreach, education and memorials, but not direct payments.

connections.label: Isaac Royall Jr. endowed first law professorship

records.name: Yale and Slavery Research Project (2020–2024)
records.description: Launched in 2020 and led by historian David Blight; its 2024 book 'Yale and Slavery: A History' found that founders and early leaders enslaved over 200 people and that Connecticut Hall was partly built with enslaved labour. Yale formally apologised on 16 February 2024 and funded free copies and local programmes in New Haven.

records.name: University of Glasgow reparative justice programme
records.description: A September 2018 report by Simon Newman and Stephen Mullen found Glasgow received gifts from slavery-derived wealth worth c. £16.7m–£198m today, though it never owned enslaved people. In August 2019 it signed an agreement with the University of the West Indies to raise £20m over 20 years for a Glasgow-Caribbean Centre for Development Research, widely called the first such UK university commitment.

connections.label: agreement backed by Sir Hilary Beckles (UWI)

records.name: University of Cambridge Legacies of Enslavement inquiry (2019–2022)
records.description: Set up in 2019; its report of 22 September 2022 found Cambridge gained 'significant benefits' from slavery through investments in the South Sea Company, donations from investors in slave-trading companies, and fellows' roles, while finding no evidence it owned enslaved people or plantations. Colleges such as Jesus and Christ's ran their own inquiries.

records.name: Princeton & Slavery Project (2017)
records.description: Research project led by historian Martha Sandweiss, launched publicly in November 2017, which found that Princeton's first nine presidents all owned enslaved people at some point, documented a 1766 slave auction on campus, and traced donor wealth such as Moses Taylor Pyne's Cuban-sugar inheritance.

records.name: Evanston, Illinois, local reparations programme (2021)
records.description: In March 2021 Evanston's council voted 8–1 to begin the first US city reparations programme, funded by a 3% cannabis tax pledged in 2019 (target $10m over ten years). It gives eligible Black residents or descendants who suffered housing discrimination between 1919 and 1969 $25,000 for housing costs; it addresses housing discrimination rather than slavery directly.

records.name: California Reparations Task Force (AB 3121)
records.description: Created by California's AB 3121 (2020), the first US state task force on reparations. Its c. 1,100-page final report of 29 June 2023 made more than 115 recommendations, including a formal apology and methods for calculating compensation for descendants of enslaved people; the legislature has since enacted only some measures.

records.name: H.R. 40 — Commission to Study and Develop Reparation Proposals
records.description: Bill first introduced by Rep. John Conyers in 1989 and reintroduced every Congress since, to create a 13-member commission studying slavery and its legacy and recommending remedies. On 14 April 2021 the House Judiciary Committee approved it 25–17, its first-ever committee vote; it has not passed the full House.

connections.label: courts called reparations a political question

events.title: Barings and Hope finance the Louisiana Purchase
events.text: Barings (60%) and Hope & Co. bought the US bonds used to pay Napoleon, opening a vast territory to cotton and sugar slavery.

events.title: Moss brothers move enslaved people to Demerara
events.text: John and Henry Moss bought Anna Regina and shipped hundreds of people they had inherited in the Bahamas to work it; 603 were moved under licence in 1821–25.

events.title: Haiti's indemnity payable to the Caisse des Dépôts

events.title: Barings sells Louisiana planter-bank bonds
events.text: Barings marketed c. $2.5m in bonds of the Consolidated Association of the Planters of Louisiana, whose capital rested on mortgaged land and enslaved people.
